newsitem.title: USA: American Airlines-pilots labor talks extended.
newsitem.headline: American Airlines-pilots labor talks extended.

text.p: President Clinton delayed for two days a mediator's report on the labor dispute between American Airlines and its pilots, raising hope that a settlement could be reached without a strike, the White House said Monday.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Clinton extended the report's deadline from Monday at the request of Presidential Emergency Board Chairman Robert Harris, who said the extra days could help to resolve the dispute.

He said Harris told Clinton that the two sides were "engaged in intensive mediation meetings and that additional time prior to the board's submission of its report will increase the likelihood of a successful outcome."

American, a unit of AMR Corp., the nation's No. 2 airline, and the Allied Pilots Association resumed talks on Friday, their first meeting since Feb. 14, when a week of intensive talks broke down without an agreement.

The APA's 9,300 members went on strike but Clinton immediately created the emergency board to try to resolve the dispute over wages and whether American will use APA pilots or other pilots to fly new small commuter jets for its regional carrier, American Eagle.

Under federal labor law governing airlines, Clinton's action stopped the pilots from striking and stopped American from locking the pilots out for 60 days while the board drew up a proposed settlement and the two sides considered it.
McCurry also said American and the APA agreed to extend the 60-day period to April 28, two weeks beyond the original deadline.
If a voluntary solution is not reached by April 28, the pilots could strike or American could lock them out.

McCurry said "the president compliments both American and the Allied Pilots Association on this agreement and their willingness to engage in these mediation efforts. He encourages them to redouble these efforts to reach a negotiated settlement."
McCurry said he would not speculate on whether any progress was being made, but noted that the two sides had asked for the additional time so they could resolve their dispute "in a peaceful manner."
During the past month, Harris and the two other members of the emergency board took testimony from American and the pilots in preparation for their report to Clinton on how to resolve the dispute.
But Harris had said he would step in to mediate at any point if he thought he could resolve the dispute before submitting his report to the president.
After the April 28 deadline, Congress could step in to force the pilots back to work in case of a strike, or order the two sides to accept the board's proposals or enter arbitration.
On wages, the union wants an 11 percent increase to cover the last three years, when it got no raises, and the next four. American has offered 6.5 percent.

The union also wants its members, who earn an average of $120,000 a year, in the cockpits of the new smaller jets. But American says it cannot compete with other commuter carriers unless the new jets are flown by the lower-paid American Eagle pilots.
